Where it began

Ian Jonathan Leonard Trott was born in Cape Town on 22 April 1981, into a South African family with English roots. His grandfather had been born in London, which gave young Jonathan a British passport from birth. He went to Rondebosch Boys' High School and Stellenbosch University, and played for South Africa at under-15 and under-19 level. His half-brother, Kenny Jackson, also played the game seriously, for Western Province and the Netherlands.

He soon found a home at Warwickshire. On his second-team debut in 2002 he made a record 245, and a year later he marked his first County Championship match with 134. That same summer he took 7 for 39 with his occasional seamers, the only five-wicket haul of his first-class career. In 2005 he made four hundreds for the county, the biggest of them 210 against Sussex.

The player

England called him up for the deciding Ashes Test at the Oval in 2009. He made 41 in the first innings and 119 in the second, becoming the 18th Englishman to score a hundred on Test debut. England won the match and the Ashes. Tottenham Hotspur, the football club he had always followed, sent him a signed shirt by way of congratulations.

The big scores kept coming. He made 226 against Bangladesh at Lord's in May 2010, and in that game he also picked up his first Test wicket. Later that summer, also at Lord's, he made 184 against Pakistan and shared an eighth-wicket stand of 332 with Stuart Broad, a world record. In Australia that winter he made 135 not out at Brisbane and 168 not out at Melbourne, where England kept the Ashes. In 2011 his 203 at Cardiff was, at the time, the highest score by an Englishman against Sri Lanka.

In 52 Tests from 2009 to 2015 he made 3,835 runs at 44.08, with nine hundreds and 19 fifties, and held 29 catches.

What made him special

He was a right-handed top-order batsman built for long innings, as his two Test double hundreds show. With Alastair Cook and Andrew Strauss he formed the top three of a strong England side, and in 2011 he helped them reach first place in the Test rankings.

He was not one for the big hit, though. By March 2013 nobody in Test cricket had made more runs without hitting a six. His medium pace was a gentler weapon: five Test wickets at 80 each.

Away from the middle

2011 was his year. He was a Wisden Cricketer of the Year, England's Cricketer of the Year and the ICC Cricketer of the Year. He won the Ashes three times, in 2009, 2010/11 and 2013. His England career ended in 2015, and he finished as a professional cricketer in 2018. In July 2022 he took over as head coach of Afghanistan.

And finally

Plenty of batsmen have dreamt of a debut hundred in an Ashes decider. Very few have been sent a football shirt for it. For a lifelong Tottenham fan, that may have been the sweetest part.
